introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Further Mathematics Paper 2 (0775), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Answer ALL 10 questions. For your guidance, the approximate mark allocation for parts of each question is indicated. Mathematical formulae and tables published by the Board, and noiseless non-programmable electronic calculators are allowed. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

Question 10 (iv)-(v) : f redéfinie par f(1) = 1 ; la dérivée de la fonction prolongée en 1 vaut -1/2 (développement de ln au voisinage de 1), valeur donnée dans le tableau de variation.

questions.corrige_markdown:
Two conditions must hold:

- $\ln x$ is defined only for $x > 0$;
- the denominator must not vanish: $x - 1 \neq 0$, so $x \neq 1$.

$$\boxed{D_f = (0, 1) \cup (1, +\infty) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : x > 0,\ x \neq 1\}}$$

**As $x \to 0^+$.** $\ln x \to -\infty$ and $x - 1 \to -1$. A very large negative number divided by a number close to $-1$ is very large and positive:

$$\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x) = +\infty.$$

**As $x \to 1$.** The numerator and denominator both tend to $0$. Recognise the definition of the derivative of $\ln$ at $1$:

$$\lim_{x\to1}\frac{\ln x - \ln 1}{x - 1} = \left.\frac{d}{dx}\ln x\right|_{x=1} = \frac11 = 1.$$

$$\lim_{x\to1}f(x) = 1.$$

**As $x \to \infty$.** Write $f(x) = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 - \frac1x}$. Since $\dfrac{\ln x}{x} \to 0$ (the logarithm grows more slowly than any positive power of $x$) and $\dfrac{1}{1 - 1/x} \to 1$,

$$\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x) = 0.$$

$$\boxed{+\infty,\quad 1,\quad 0}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: Hence or otherwise, find the asymptotes to the curve $y = f(x)$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
- As $x \to 0^+$, $f(x) \to +\infty$: the line $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis) is a **vertical asymptote**.
- As $x \to +\infty$, $f(x) \to 0$: the line $y = 0$ (the $x$-axis) is a **horizontal asymptote**.
- At $x = 1$ the limit is the finite number $1$, so there is **no** asymptote there: the curve has only a missing point (a hole) at $(1, 1)$.

$$\boxed{x = 0 \text{ (vertical)} \quad\text{and}\quad y = 0 \text{ (horizontal, as } x\to+\infty)}$$

(The function is not defined for $x < 0$, so there is no behaviour to study as $x \to -\infty$.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Redefine $f$ so that it is continuous at $x = 1$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
$f$ is not defined at $x = 1$, but $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}f(x) = 1$ exists and is finite (part ii). Defining the value at $1$ to be this limit removes the discontinuity:

$$\boxed{f(x) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{\ln x}{x - 1}, & x > 0,\ x \neq 1,\\[2mm] 1, & x = 1.\end{cases}}$$

Then $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}f(x) = 1 = f(1)$, so $f$ is continuous at $x = 1$, hence on $(0, +\infty)$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Furthermore, using the relationship $\dfrac{1}{x} + \ln x \geq 1$, investigate $f$ and draw its variation table. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Derivative.** For $x > 0$, $x \neq 1$, by the quotient rule

$$f'(x) = \frac{\frac1x(x-1) - \ln x}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{1 - \frac1x - \ln x}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{1 - \left(\frac1x + \ln x\right)}{(x-1)^2}.$$

**Sign.** The given relationship $\dfrac1x + \ln x \geq 1$ makes the numerator $1 - \left(\dfrac1x + \ln x\right) \leq 0$, and $(x-1)^2 > 0$. Hence $f'(x) \leq 0$ on each interval of the domain.

(The relationship itself comes from $g(x) = \dfrac1x + \ln x$, $g'(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{x^2}$, which has its minimum $g(1) = 1$. So $g(x) > 1$ for $x \neq 1$ and in fact $f'(x) < 0$ for $x \neq 1$.)

At $x = 1$, for the continuous extension of part (iv), the expansion $\ln x = (x-1) - \dfrac{(x-1)^2}{2} + \cdots$ gives $f(x) = 1 - \dfrac{x-1}{2} + \cdots$, so $f'(1) = -\dfrac12 < 0$ as well.

**Conclusion.** $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0, +\infty)$. Also $f(x) > 0$ for all $x > 0$ (numerator and denominator have the same sign).

**Variation table.**

| $x$ | $0$ | | $1$ | | $+\infty$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f'(x)$ | | $-$ | $-\tfrac12$ | $-$ | |
| $f(x)$ | $+\infty$ | $\searrow$ | $1$ | $\searrow$ | $0$ |

questions.enonce_markdown: Sketch the curve of $y = f(x)$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Features to show.**

- Domain $x > 0$: the curve lies entirely to the right of the $y$-axis, in the first quadrant ($f > 0$).
- The $y$-axis ($x = 0$) is a vertical asymptote: $f \to +\infty$ as $x \to 0^+$.
- The curve passes through $(1, 1)$ (the continuous extension) with gradient $-\tfrac12$ there.
- The curve is strictly decreasing and tends to the horizontal asymptote $y = 0$ as $x \to +\infty$ without ever reaching it.
- No intersection with the axes: there is no $x$-intercept ($\ln x = 0$ only at $x = 1$, where $f = 1$).

**Table of values.**

| $x$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $2$ | $5$ | $10$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | $2.56$ | $1.39$ | $1$ | $0.69$ | $0.40$ | $0.26$ |

**Shape.** Start very high along the $y$-axis near $x = 0$, fall steeply through $(0.5, 1.39)$ and $(1, 1)$, then flatten out, decreasing slowly towards the $x$-axis as $x$ grows.
